slides.title: Operational Models
slides.notes: Open by framing Chapter 17 as a design checkpoint rather than a new construction recipe. The class has seen several models, so the question is now how to choose among them. Emphasize that the source span is short because it synthesizes the whole Part II strategy.

slides.title: Covariance Test
slides.notes: Use the square as the governing test for every model in the lecture. If an object is constructed from inputs and then transformed, the result should agree with transforming the inputs first and reconstructing. That is what makes a representation operational instead of merely coordinate storage.

slides.title: Model Contract Matrix
slides.notes: Read the table horizontally. Each model earns its place by making some objects, operators, and predicates native. The point is not that one column dominates. The point is that every implementation must state what it promises before users start measuring accidental coordinate artifacts.

slides.title: Representation Lifts
slides.notes: Walk upward through the ladder and ask what each added coordinate or constraint buys. A lift is justified when it turns the required transformations into simple algebraic actions or makes the desired predicates invariant. Without that payoff, extra coordinates are just extra testing burden.

slides.title: Vector-Space Route
slides.notes: Treat the vector-space model as the lean baseline, not a primitive leftover. It is excellent when the task is angular, directional, or fixed-origin. Rotors and orthogonal maps preserve the metric on directions, but finite translations and incidence need bookkeeping outside the native model.

slides.title: Homogeneous Route
slides.notes: Point out that homogeneous coordinates are not only a computer-graphics convention. They make affine and projective transformations linear, and they make join and meet operations uniform. The tradeoff is equally important: the raw coordinate dot product is not Euclidean distance.

slides.title: Plucker Route
slides.notes: Use Plucker coordinates as the line-first cousin of the homogeneous story. A ray or line can carry direction and moment together, so line incidence and closest-approach tests become first-class. It is powerful for cameras and robotics, but it is not a universal metric model of points.

slides.title: Conformal Route
slides.notes: Present conformal geometry as the route that pays two null directions to make distance and round objects algebraic. The same operator pattern can move points, lines, circles, spheres, and planes. The cost is a larger representation and stricter metric discipline.

slides.title: Other Operational Models
slides.notes: This slide is deliberately speculative, matching the chapter's forward-looking tone. Image, projective, and contact geometries suggest that operational models are a method, not a finished catalog. The right question is which invariants and transformations deserve to be native for the application.

slides.title: Routing Decisions
slides.notes: Run the decision chart as a live diagnostic. Begin with the workload, identify the objects that must survive transformations, then route by native predicates and operator cost. The class should see model choice as an engineering decision with tests, not a matter of taste.

slides.title: Tradeoff Heatmap
slides.notes: The heatmap compresses the same idea into a review artifact. A high score means the model makes the requirement natural; a low score means conversions or special cases are likely. Ask students where their own application would sit before choosing a default algebra.

slides.title: Predicate Discipline
slides.notes: Use the testing harness to prevent a common mistake: measuring the representation space as though it were automatically physical space. Each model has predicates that are meaningful and coordinate quantities that are merely storage artifacts. Good software names and tests that boundary explicitly.

slides.title: Implementation Bridge
slides.notes: Connect Chapter 17 to the next part of the book. Once the operational contract is chosen, implementation work becomes basis choices, product tables, specialized kernels, and validation. The algebraic elegance matters only if the resulting code preserves the promised operations efficiently.

slides.title: Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close by making the routing habit memorable. Start from operators, choose the representation that makes them native, name the predicates that are invariant, and write checks that fail when the wrong model is used. That is the practical lesson of operational models.
